idiom_name: package-private monitor inside internal/, invoked from middleware, with the principal carried in context.Context
implementation_notes: Go has no access modifiers, but it has two boundaries that together replace the classic structure: an identifier whose first character is not an upper-case letter is reachable only from its own package, and since Go 1.4 the go command refuses to let code outside the subtree rooted at the parent of an internal directory import packages inside it. The monitor therefore becomes a package under internal/ that exports one small decision API, with the protected state unexported and not constructible from outside the package, while middleware on the request path supplies the always-invoked property. What the language cannot provide is tamper resistance - unsafe, reflect and //go:linkname reach unexported state from anywhere in the same binary - so the deployment boundary (a separate process, a container, an OS sandbox) is what protects the monitor from code that must not bypass it.
pitfalls: The internal rule is subtree-wide, not monitor-only: every package in the same module subtree may import the monitor, including the code it is meant to constrain, so keep the exported surface to the decision function and let adversary-facing code live in another module.

Unexported state is not unreachable: unsafe, reflect and //go:linkname can obtain and mutate it from a package in the same binary, so in-process enforcement in Go is a convention with teeth rather than a sandbox.

Middleware is only as complete as its registration: handlers mounted on a bare mux, or registered before the wrapper is applied, never reach the monitor, and a goroutine started with context.Background() carries no principal at all.
Copying the protected value out (an exported struct, or a slice that aliases internal storage) hands the caller an unmediated object; return copies or accessors that re-check.
